title: Distance-Dependent Stability of Continuous-Time QuantumWalks on Watts-Strogatz Networks: The Role of Global Geometric Centrality
content: The stability of continuous-time quantum walks (CTQWs) under environmental decoherence is a foundational factor in quantum transport and algorithm design. Prior work has reported that coherence lifetime correlates with shortest-path distance d from the network hub and has emphasized the centrality of the initialization node—including local degree and local topological features—as the structural driver of this correlation. We test this hypothesis rigorously using full fourth-order Runge–Kutta (RK4) integration of the Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad master equation. For the quantum stochastic walk (QSW) channel, we simulate N = 100 nodes per realization across ten independent realizations for each of Watts–Strogatz (WS), Barab´asi–Albert (BA), and Erd˝os–R´enyi (ER) topologies, yielding 3000 node-level relaxation times. Shell-level HS and intrinsic- Milburn data are used as qualitative cross-checks. We find that the WS distance effect is not confounded by local degree: the partial correlation after degree control is ρ(d|k) = +0.30 (p = 3 × 10−22), essentially unchanged from the raw value (ρ = +0.30; −0.8% attenuation). Neighbour degree also carries negligible explanatory power at the population level. For WS-QSW, a twelve- test systematic exploration instead identifies global geometric centrality as the primary explanatory covariate. Closeness centrality alone attenuates the distance coefficient to non-significance (βd = 5× 10−5, p = 0.99; 99.9% reduction); resistance distance attenuates it by 88.7%. Both covariates survive neighbour-degree control and remain independently significant in a combined model (βR = +0.65, p = 2 × 10−7; βc = −13.1, p = 7 × 10−68). These conclusions are robust to the definitional overlap between closeness centrality and hub distance: hub-excluded closeness reproduces the attenuation (βd reduction 93.8%, pd = 0.52). The practical magnitude is substantial: closeness centrality alone explains 37.5% of the rank variance in the relaxation time, and the difference between the highest- and lowest-closeness deciles corresponds to a 26.7% change in coherence lifetime. Five-fold group cross-validation confirms that this predictive performance generalizes to held-out realizations (CV-R2 rises from 0.07 at baseline to 0.36 for the full geometric model). A rewiring-probability sweep shows that the WS distance effect is absent at p = 0 (perfect-ring symmetry), peaks at p = 0.01 (sparse shortcuts), and decreases monotonically as p → 1, identifying shortcut-induced geometric asymmetry as the structural origin. Real-network validation on four standard networks shows that closeness centrality is the only covariate with a consistent negative correlation with τ in every network (ρ = −0.37 to −0.57, p < 0.05), whereas hub distance varies in sign. Finally, transport efficiency to a fixed target shows a strong opposite dependence (ρ(closeness, η) = +0.44, p < 10−24), revealing a model-specific empirical coherence–transport trade-off: peripheral nodes preserve coherence longer (by 27% in the extreme deciles) but transport 79% less efficiently than central nodes. We recommend reporting closeness centrality and resistance distance as the primary explanatory covariates for CTQW stability on WS networks, and treating local degree as a secondary structural diagnostic.
